Prepare Kernel Inputs for Scale Optimization

Source: R/kernel_prep.R
kernel_prep.Rd

Extracts the raster cells around each survey point, records the distance from the point to each cell, and computes a first set of kernel-weighted covariates. Fit your starting model to those covariates, then pass the model and the returned object to multiScale_optim(). This is the first step of every multiScaleR workflow, shown in vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR").

Usage

kernel_prep(
  pts,
  raster_stack,
  max_D,
  kernel = c("gaussian", "exp", "expow", "fixed"),
  scale_vars = NULL,
  sigma = NULL,
  shape = NULL,
  projected = TRUE,
  progress = FALSE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  bin = TRUE,
  nbins = 256L,
  store_cell_data = TRUE
)

Arguments

pts

Survey point locations as a SpatVector (terra) or sf object, in a projected coordinate system whose units match max_D. Row names are kept as point IDs.

raster_stack

A SpatRaster (terra) with one or more layers, on the same projection as pts. Without scale_vars, each layer becomes a covariate with the layer's name, so the names must match the model formula. Layer names cannot be "x", which is reserved for internal coordinate data. The raster must cover a buffer of max_D around every point.

max_D

Positive numeric scalar. Radius, in map units, of the circle around each point within which raster cells are extracted. It is also the upper bound of the sigma search, and kernels are cut off at this distance. Set it above the largest plausible scale of effect, at least about 3.3 times the largest plausible sigma for a Gaussian kernel. If an estimate comes back near max_D, increase it and run kernel_prep() again. See the section on choosing max_D in multiScaleR-kernels.

kernel

Character. Distance-weighting function used for every covariate: "gaussian" (default), "exp" (negative exponential), "expow" (exponential power, which also estimates a shape), or "fixed" (equal weight within a radius). The weight functions are given in multiScaleR-kernels. To compare kernels, run kernel_prep() once per kernel.

scale_vars

Optional covariate specifications created with msr_vars(). Omit it to make each raster layer one kernel-weighted mean. Supply it to define derived covariates, such as a kernel mean and a landscape or surface metric from the same layer.

sigma

Optional numeric vector of starting sigma values, in map units, one per covariate whose scale is estimated (one per raster layer when scale_vars is omitted). Default: NULL, which starts every sigma at max_D / 2. The default is recommended. These values set the covariates in kernel_dat and are not the starting values of multiScale_optim(), which chooses its own.

shape

Optional numeric vector of starting shape values for kernel = "expow", with the same length as sigma. Default: NULL, which starts every shape at 2 (the Gaussian form). Ignored for other kernels.

projected

Logical. Whether pts and raster_stack use projected (planar) coordinates. Only projected coordinates are supported, so FALSE is an error. Default: TRUE.

progress

Logical. Show progress bars during extraction and weighting. Default: FALSE.

verbose

Logical. Print status messages. Default: TRUE.

bin

Logical. If TRUE (default), summarize each kernel mean's cell values into distance bins. multiScale_optim() then evaluates kernel means from the bins instead of every cell, which is much faster and no longer depends on max_D, at the cost of a negligible approximation. The analytic backends and multiScale_bayes() require it for kernel means. With the default refit backend it also bins kernel-weighted surface metrics (surface_var(weighted = TRUE) with "sq", "ssk", or "sku"): each cell's centered value powers are split between the two nearest distance nodes, which keeps their approximation as small as that of a binned kernel mean. Weighted "sa", kernel = "fixed", landscape metrics, and hard-radius surface metrics are never binned, and the analytic backends and multiScale_bayes() evaluate weighted surface metrics from every cell. FALSE forces exact cell-by-cell evaluation.

nbins

Integer, at least 2. Number of equal-width distance bins when bin = TRUE. More bins increase accuracy and memory. The default (256) reproduces exact optimization results to several significant figures. Ignored when bin = FALSE.

store_cell_data

Logical. If TRUE (default), the per-cell distances (d_list) and values (raw_cov) are kept. If FALSE, they are dropped after binning, often shrinking the object by one to two orders of magnitude. This lean mode needs bin = TRUE and only kernel means. With landscape or surface metrics, or bin = FALSE, the cell data are kept and a message says so. The bins suffice for optimization, profile_sigma(), and the final refit.

Value

An object of class multiScaleR_data, a list. Its full structure is described in multiScaleR_data. The parts you use directly:

  • kernel_dat: data frame with one row per point and one column per covariate. Values are centered and scaled (mean 0, standard deviation 1) at the starting sigma. Combine it with your response data to fit the starting model.

  • scl_params: list with the mean and sd used for that scaling, in the covariates' own units.

  • kernel, max_D, min_D, and scale_vars: the settings passed on to multiScale_optim() and kernel_scale.raster().

Printing the object reports the number of points and covariates, the kernel, the number of cells extracted around the first point ("Number of elements"), whether binning is on, the minimum distance (min_D, about one cell width and the lower bound of the sigma search), the maximum distance (max_D), and the unit conversion (distances are stored divided by max_D).

Prepare the points and rasters

Points and rasters must share a defined, projected CRS. Every distance, including max_D and any sigma you supply, is in the linear unit of that projection, usually meters. Landscape and surface metrics also need square cells. Row names of pts are kept throughout, so model data can be joined back to the points.

Each point's buffer is the circle of radius max_D, and every cell it intersects is extracted, including partly covered boundary cells, which keep their full kernel weight. Missing cells drop out of each weighted mean, and the remaining weights renormalize. Extraction runs in batches of 25 points to limit the peak memory of temporary tables. Point order, returned values, and distances are not affected.

Manage memory

A larger max_D extracts more cells per point. Check the size of the object and the memory needed for parallel optimization with estimate_multiscale_ram(). When every covariate is a kernel mean, store_cell_data = FALSE keeps only the bins.

Related preparation functions

To assign each observation to a different annual raster while estimating one pooled landscape relationship, use kernel_prep_by_group(). To prepare inputs for unmarked models, see prepare_unmarked_data().

See also

multiScale_optim(), msr_vars(), multiScaleR-kernels, multiScaleR_data, estimate_multiscale_ram(). vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR") explains each argument on a worked example.

Examples

## Survey points and a binary habitat raster bundled with the package
data("pts")
data("count_data")
hab <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "hab.tif",
                               package = "multiScaleR"))

kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts,
                             raster_stack = hab,
                             max_D = 250,          # map units (meters)
                             kernel = "gaussian",
                             verbose = FALSE)
# 75 points, one covariate, cells within 250 m of each point
kernel_inputs
#> 
#> There are 75 observations at 1 spatial covariate(s): 
#> hab
#> 
#> The specified kernel is:
#> gaussian
#> 
#> Number of elements: 
#> 2052
#> Distance binning:
#> enabled (256 distance bins per covariate)
#> Minimum Distance:
#> 10
#> Maximum Distance:
#> 250
#> Unit Conversion:
#> 250

# Standardized kernel-weighted habitat at the starting sigma (125 m)
head(kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
#>          hab
#> 1 -0.4206979
#> 2  1.7520402
#> 3  0.5073754
#> 4 -0.8959421
#> 5 -0.1734359
#> 6  0.8108489

# Fit the starting model that multiScale_optim() will optimize
df <- data.frame(count_data["y"], kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
mod <- glm(y ~ hab, family = poisson, data = df)

## Lean mode keeps only the distance bins
lean_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = hab, max_D = 250,
                           store_cell_data = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
# Object sizes in megabytes
c(full = as.numeric(object.size(kernel_inputs)),
  lean = as.numeric(object.size(lean_inputs))) / 1e6
#>     full     lean 
#> 2.547720 0.328272
